config.title: Concurrent Mode Gotchas

intro.title: Concurrent Mode Gotchas
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that demonstrates common pitfalls when using Concurrent Mode features like `useTransition` and `useDeferredValue`. You will learn how to manage state updates that might cause visual glitches or performance issues during rendering. The core concept is understanding how React's Concurrent Mode allows for interruptible rendering and how to structure your code to avoid conflicts. You will use React hooks, TypeScript for type safety, and controlled state to create a smooth user experience. By the end, you'll know how to write components that are resilient to rendering interruptions.
intro.usecase: Concurrent Mode patterns appear in complex dashboards where multiple data visualizations update simultaneously, like financial trading platforms or real-time analytics tools. They're crucial for interactive forms with dependent fields that trigger validation or API calls while users continue typing, preventing UI freezes. You'll encounter these patterns in e-commerce filtering systems where price ranges, categories, and search terms update product grids without blocking user interactions. Understanding these gotchas helps developers build responsive admin panels where data fetching, sorting, and editing operations happen concurrently without disrupting the user experience.

objectives: Apply the useTransition hook to mark non-urgent state updates and prevent UI blocking.
Use the useDeferredValue hook to defer rendering of non-critical UI components.
Implement Suspense boundaries to handle loading states for asynchronous components.
Execute conditional rendering to display fallback content while components are loading.
Utilize the startTransition API to wrap state updates that should yield to user interactions.
Construct error boundaries to catch and handle errors in concurrent components.
Define component structures that separate urgent and non-urgent updates for better user experience.
Invoke the useMemo hook to memoize expensive calculations and prevent unnecessary re-renders.
Control rendering priority by wrapping components with Suspense and providing appropriate fallbacks.
Modify existing state updates to use concurrent features for improved application responsiveness.
Access the isPending flag from useTransition to show loading indicators during transitions.
Compare synchronous and concurrent rendering approaches to identify performance bottlenecks.

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to import multiple named exports from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React and useState is added at the top of the file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState, which are essential for building React components with state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package using the correct syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package using an import statement.

steps.title: Create the main component function
steps.instruction: Create a function component named ConcurrentDemo that returns JSX.Element. Use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Start by defining the component function. Remember to include the return type annotation : JSX.Element for TypeScript.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the ConcurrentDemo component function here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named ConcurrentDemo is defined with a return type of JSX.Element.
successCriteria: The component function is named ConcurrentDemo, returns JSX.Element, and is syntactically correct in TypeScript.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the ConcurrentDemo component with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the component 'ConcurrentDemo'? Did you specify the return type ': JSX.Element'?
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Make sure you define a function named ConcurrentDemo that returns JSX.Element.

steps.title: Initialize count state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside the ConcurrentDemo component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'count' initialized to 0. This will track the number of clicks.
steps.hint: Remember to destructure useState from React. The syntax is: const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a numeric state variable
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a count state variable initialized to 0 with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the count state with proper TypeScript typing. This will track the number of clicks in our concurrent mode demonstration.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the state variable 'count'? Did you initialize it to 0? Did you include the TypeScript type annotation <number>?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the ConcurrentDemo component, use useState to create a state variable named 'count' initialized to 0 with TypeScript typing.

steps.title: Initialize loading state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside your ConcurrentDemo component, add a second useState hook to create a loading state variable initialized to false. Use TypeScript to explicitly type it as boolean.
steps.hint: Call useState<boolean>(false) and destructure the returned array into a variable (e.g., loading) and its setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a boolean state variable
const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a loading state variable (initialized to false) and its setter function, ready to track loading status.
successCriteria: The code includes a useState<boolean>(false) call, destructured into two variables (e.g., loading and setLoading).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a loading state with the correct boolean type.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you use useState<boolean>(false) and destructure both the state variable and setter?
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. Remember to call useState<boolean>(false) and destructure the result into two variables.

steps.title: Define the simulateFetch handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your ConcurrentDemo component, define an async function named simulateFetch that will simulate a network request. This function should update both the loading and count states.
steps.hint: Create an async function that uses the setLoading and setCount functions from useState. You can simulate a delay with setTimeout or await new Promise.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an async simulateFetch function defined inside your component that will eventually handle loading and count state updates.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've defined the simulateFetch handler function. This async function will help demonstrate concurrency issues when we call it multiple times.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but make sure it's async and properly handles the loading and count state updates. Check that you're using setLoading and setCount inside the function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The simulateFetch function isn't defined correctly. Make sure to create an async function inside your component that will update both loading and count states.

steps.title: Define the resetCount handler function
steps.instruction: Inside the ConcurrentDemo component, define a function named resetCount that sets the count state back to 0. Place it after the simulateFetch handler (or where you would define it if simulateFetch isn't defined yet).
steps.hint: Create a function that calls setCount(0). You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a resetCount function that, when called, will reset the count state to 0.
successCriteria: The resetCount function must be defined inside the component, call setCount(0), and have proper TypeScript typing (void return type).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the resetCount handler function that will reset the count state to 0.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your resetCount function properly calls setCount(0) and has the correct TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackWrong: The resetCount function doesn't seem to be defined correctly. Make sure you create a function that calls setCount(0) to reset the count state.

steps.hint: Update the opening <div> tag to include className='concurrent-demo'.

The existing <h1> element remains inside the div
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the main container div with the correct className. This provides a CSS hook for styling the component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the div has exactly className='concurrent-demo' and that it wraps the h1 element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The container div with className 'concurrent-demo' is missing or incorrect. Update the existing div to include className='concurrent-demo'.

steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the descriptive heading to explain what this demo is about.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added an h1 element with the exact text 'Concurrent Mode Gotchas Demo' inside the container div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The heading wasn't added correctly. Please add an h1 element with the text 'Concurrent Mode Gotchas Demo' inside the container div.

steps.title: Add the fetch button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add a <button> element with the text 'Start Fetch' and wire its onClick event to call the simulateFetch handler function.
steps.hint: Remember to use the onClick prop and pass the simulateFetch function reference (without calling it).
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a button with onClick wired to a handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Start Fetch' appears in the UI, and when clicked, it will trigger the simulateFetch function (once that function is defined in a later step).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the fetch button and wired it to the simulateFetch handler. This button will trigger the async operation when clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but check: 1) Is the button text exactly 'Start Fetch'? 2) Did you wire onClick to simulateFetch (not call it)?
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly configured. Make sure you add a <button> element with text 'Start Fetch' and onClick={simulateFetch}.

steps.title: Add the reset button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Add a second button element with the text 'Reset' and wire its onClick event to call the resetCount handler function.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element after the existing fetch button. Set its text content to 'Reset' and its onClick prop to {resetCount}.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a reset button with onClick handler
<button onClick={resetCount}>Reset</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A second button labeled 'Reset' appears next to the fetch button. Clicking it will reset the count to 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the reset button with proper onClick wiring. This completes the basic UI controls for the demo.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but check: does it have the exact text 'Reset' and is onClick set to {resetCount}?
steps.feedbackWrong: The reset button is missing or not properly configured. Add a <button> element with text 'Reset' and onClick={resetCount}.
